newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Claimant to Russian throne seeks official status.
newsitem.headline: Claimant to Russian throne seeks official status.

text.p: The grandmother of one of the claimants to the Russian imperial throne said on Friday that President Boris Yeltsin had given her family a house in Moscow and that they hoped to get some official status in Russia.

Grand Duchess Leonida Georgyevna, now residing in Madrid, said the family planned a visit to Russia in June but that their permanent return depended on the government, Yeltsin and "the Russian people".
"We hope for this a great deal," said Leonida, who is in her early 80s and who has been living in exile since 1918 when the Bolsheviks shot dead the last tsar, Nicholas II, and his family.

The grand duchess is the widow of the Grand Duke Vladimir, who was a cousin of Nicholas II. Her grandson, Grand Duke Georgy Mikhailovich Romanov, 16, is one of several relatives who claims the right of inheritance.
"It depends first of all on the boy's schooling, whether he'll finish it here or not and some conditions must be met by the government on this before we decide," Leonida said.
Asked what conditions and whether she was negotiating with Moscow, she said the family wanted some kind of official role.
"My daughter would like there to be a status," she said, declining to elaborate.

Leonida was similiarly vague on the issue of the return of the monarchy. "There's a lot of talk, it is an unresolved question and only the president..and the Russian people if they want it. We do not want to get involved in politics," she said.

But pressed on her daughter's views on a political role she said: "It depends on the conditions, it's very hard to say in advance. We respect the president, we love the country and whatever the people wants, I don't know," Leonida said.

"The president gave me a house here and I like it a lot and I am always sad when I leave. I would like to stay here if possible," she said, adding that the house was near one of the president's own country dachas.
Leonida said she had had a house near Moscow for two years, although the handover has never been announced by the Kremlin.

Britain's Daily Telegraph newspaper earlier this year quoted a Kremlin source as saying Yeltsin had signed a secret decree that would officially reinstate Georgy as the head of Russia's imperial family this year, although his role would be symbolic.

The monarchist movement is very small in Russia and most people are far to preoccupied with the struggle to survive the country's post-communist economic collapse to have any strong views about the tsar and his squabbling descendants.
Some members of the imperial family regard Prince Nicholas, a wealthy landowner living in Switzerland, as the most senior in the royal line.
But Leonida, revealing some of the bitter infighting among the tsar's decendants, was scathing. "Who respects him?" she said, laughing.
